title: Macauliffe, the translator
hookLine: an Irish civil servant resigned his post to translate the Granth, working with Sikh scholars

lines: A SAFE CAREER IN THE PUNJAB.
cards: A British official in the Punjab has a safe career: a salary, a rank, a pension waiting at the end. Max Arthur Macauliffe, an Irishman in the Indian Civil Service, had all of that.
Then he did something a career like that rarely makes room for. He resigned.
He gave up the post, and the security, to spend his days sitting with Sikh scholars over the hymns of the Gurus, trying to carry them into English.

teach.h: SUNG POETRY, HARD TO CARRY OVER.
teach.b: First, what he was up against. The Guru Granth Sahib is sung poetry, in several languages and dialects, set to ragas. An earlier English translation had already come out, and Sikh critics felt it misunderstood the Gurus.
A text like that doesn't open easily to an outsider with a dictionary. Second, how he chose to work. Macauliffe didn't translate alone and announce his results.
He worked with Sikh scholars, and one name that comes up is Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha. He would put a line into English, and they would talk through what it meant to the people who sang it.

teach.h: THE COST OF LEAVING HIS POST.
teach.b: Third, the cost. Leaving the service meant giving up income and standing. Accounts of his life say he spent much of his own money on the work and died without seeing it repaid.
Whatever the exact sums, the shape of the choice is clear: a comfortable post on one side, a long, uncertain labor on the other, and he chose the labor.
Fourth, why it still matters on this path. Translations made in Macauliffe's time are old enough that anyone can now share them freely.

When a course like this one wants to quote the Gurus in English, his is one of the versions it is free to use. And there's a quieter lesson. A translator stands between two languages and belongs fully to neither.
The good ones know they need help, and ask for it.

how: Sikh readers and students still consult Macauliffe's English renderings of the Gurus' hymns, alongside modern translations and the original Gurmukhi, and his name comes up when Sikhs talk about early English translations of their scripture.

practice: Think of someone who carried something across to you from a language or a world you couldn't reach yourself: a translator of a book you love, a parent who explained the old words, a friend who interpreted at a doctor's visit.
Hold their face or their name, and let a simple thank you rest on the breath out. If you pray, say Waheguru with that person in mind.
